title: Registers, stacks and addressing modes
kicker: ENCT 303 · Computer Organization and Architecture · Chapter 2
subtitle: Instructions are bit patterns; the CPU’s registers, flags and addressing modes decide what they can reach.

sections.title: Registers and flags
sections.body:
Think of registers as the notes on a chef’s own chopping board: tiny, but within arm’s reach. Registers are the processor’s fastest memory. There are general-purpose ones, a program counter, a stack pointer, and a status register of flags set by the ALU: zero (result was 0), sign (negative), carry (unsigned overflow out of the top bit), parity and auxiliary carry. Conditional jumps test these flags.

Let’s try one: you add 0FFH + 01H in an 8-bit register and the result wraps to 00H, with a carry out. So both the zero flag and the carry flag are set: Z = 1, CY = 1, as the figure shows.

questions.prompt: After 0FFH + 01H in an 8-bit register, which flags are set?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The 8-bit result is 00H (zero), and a 1 was carried out of bit 7.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: The result is 00H, which is not negative.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Unsigned overflow is exactly what the carry flag reports.

figures.caption: Figure 2.1.1 — flags after FFH + 1
figures.note: FFH + 1 = 00H with carry out: Z = 1, CY = 1.

keynotes: Registers are the processor’s fastest memory: general-purpose ones, a program counter, a stack pointer and a status register of flags.
Flags set by the ALU: zero, sign, carry (unsigned overflow), parity and auxiliary carry; conditional jumps test them.
FFH + 1 = 00H with carry out sets Z = 1 and CY = 1.

sections.title: Stack organisation and reverse Polish notation
sections.body:
Picture a stack of plates in a canteen: you add to the top, and you take from the top. That is a stack, last in, first out. It grows in memory from the stack pointer: push writes then moves the pointer, pop moves back and reads. Calls push the return address; returns pop it, as in the figure, where CALL pushes the return address and RET pops it.

A stack machine can also evaluate reverse Polish notation directly: push operands, and each operator pops two and pushes the result. To evaluate (A+B)×C, write A B + C ×, with no parentheses and no precedence rules needed. Try 3 4 + 2 ×: push 3, push 4, then + pops both and pushes 7. Push 2; × pops 2 and 7, pushes 14. And the RPN form of A × (B + C) is A B C + ×.

worked.why: Evaluate 3 4 + 2 × in RPN with a stack.
Push 3, push 4, then + pops both and pushes 7. Push 2; × pops 2 and 7, pushes 14.

questions.prompt: The RPN form of A × (B + C) is…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Operands first, then operators in the order they are applied: B C + first, then multiply by A.

figures.caption: Figure 2.2.1 — call and return
figures.note: CALL pushes the return address; RET pops it. A ends as 0EH (7 doubled).
figures.script:
var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"cr","engine":"cpu8085","program":"LXI SP,3000H
MVI A,7
CALL DBL
HLT
DBL: ADD A
RET","memory":"","watch":"","width":600,"height":440});

keynotes: A stack grows in memory from the stack pointer: push writes then moves the pointer, pop moves back and reads.
Calls push the return address and returns pop it.
Reverse Polish notation: push operands and each operator pops two and pushes the result; 3 4 + 2 × gives 14.

sections.title: Instruction formats
sections.body:
You can think of an instruction as a short word with a job to name (the opcode) and, optionally, places to find its data. How many places? That is the design choice. Three-address instructions (ADD R1,R2,R3) are compact in program length. Two-address overwrite one source. One-address use an implicit accumulator. Zero-address use the stack. Fewer addresses make each instruction shorter but need more instructions.

See the trade. Compute X = (A+B)×(C+D) on each machine type. Three-address: ADD R1,A,B; ADD R2,C,D; MUL X,R1,R2, which is 3 instructions. One-address (accumulator): LOAD A; ADD B; STORE T; LOAD C; ADD D; MUL T; STORE X, which is 7. Which format needs no operand fields for arithmetic? The zero-address (stack) format.

worked.why: Compute X = (A+B)×(C+D) on each machine type.
Three-address: ADD R1,A,B; ADD R2,C,D; MUL X,R1,R2 → 3 instructions. One-address (accumulator): LOAD A; ADD B; STORE T; LOAD C; ADD D; MUL T; STORE X → 7.

questions.prompt: Which format needs no operand fields for arithmetic instructions?

choices.text: Zero-address (stack) — the operands are implicit on top of the stack.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It names one operand; the accumulator is the other.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Only push/pop name a memory address.

keynotes: An instruction word holds an opcode and zero to three operand fields.
Three-address is compact in program length, two-address overwrites one source, one-address uses an implicit accumulator and zero-address uses the stack.
X = (A+B)×(C+D) takes 3 instructions on a three-address machine and 7 on a one-address machine.

sections.title: Addressing modes
sections.body:
How does an instruction say where its data is? There are several ways, from pointing to the value itself to pointing to a pointer. Immediate: the value is in the instruction (MVI A,05H). Direct: the instruction holds the address (LDA 2050H). Register: the operand is in a register (MOV A,B). Register indirect: a register holds the address (MOV A,M uses HL). Indexed or base-relative: address = register + offset, ideal for arrays.

Each trades instruction length and speed for flexibility. If you want to step through an array, indexed addressing makes it easiest, because you simply change the register as you go. The figure runs four of the modes in one program.

questions.prompt: Which mode makes stepping through an array easiest?

choices.text: Register indirect or indexed — increment the register to move to the next element.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The value is fixed in the instruction.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The instruction stays the same; only the register changes.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: The address is fixed in the instruction.

figures.caption: Figure 2.4.1 — four addressing modes
figures.note: Immediate, direct, register and register-indirect in one program.
figures.script:
var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"modes","engine":"cpu8085","program":"MVI A,05H
LDA 2050H
MOV B,A
LXI H,2051H
MOV C,M
HLT","memory":"2050=0A;2051=0C","watch":"2050,2051","width":600,"height":440});

problems.prompt: What is left in A after MVI B,5 / MVI A,0 / LOOP: ADD B / DCR B / JNZ LOOP?
problems.answer: The loop adds 5+4+3+2+1 = 15 (= 0FH) and exits when B reaches zero (Z = 1).

LOOP: ADD B

keynotes: Immediate: the value is in the instruction (MVI A,05H); direct: the instruction holds the address (LDA 2050H); register: the operand is in a register (MOV A,B).
Register indirect: a register holds the address (MOV A,M uses HL); indexed or base-relative: address = register + offset, ideal for arrays.
Each mode trades instruction length and speed for flexibility.

sections.title: Interrupts
sections.body:
Your phone rings while you are reading. You bookmark the page, answer, then return to exactly the same line. A CPU does the same thing. An interrupt diverts the CPU to an interrupt service routine (ISR) when a device needs attention, an error occurs, or a timer fires.

Between instructions the CPU checks for one; if accepted it saves the program counter and flags, jumps to the ISR (found through a vector table), runs it, and returns to exactly where it left off. The interrupted program never notices. So when is an interrupt normally accepted? Between instructions, never in the middle of one.

questions.prompt: When is an interrupt normally accepted?

choices.text: Between instructions, never in the middle of one.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: That keeps the machine state consistent so the program can resume cleanly.

figures.caption: Figure 2.5.1 — interrupt handling
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Program] as p
[CPU] as c
[ISR] as i
p -> c : executing instruction n
c -> c : interrupt pending? yes
c -> i : save PC + flags, jump to vector
i --> c : service device, return
c --> p : resume at instruction n+1");

keynotes: An interrupt diverts the CPU to an interrupt service routine when a device needs attention, an error occurs or a timer fires.
Between instructions the CPU checks for one; if accepted it saves the program counter and flags, jumps to the ISR through a vector table, runs it and returns.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
One glance back at the chapter.

  • Flags record ALU outcomes; jumps read them.
  • Stacks serve calls, returns and RPN evaluation.
  • Fewer address fields mean shorter instructions but more of them.
  • Addressing modes choose how an operand is found.
keynotes: Flags record ALU outcomes and jumps read them.
Stacks serve calls, returns and RPN evaluation.
Fewer address fields mean shorter instructions but more of them, and addressing modes choose how an operand is found.
